subject: Science
title: Life Processes
summary: The chapter covers the four maintenance functions that keep an organism alive: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion, in plants, in simple animals and in human beings. It is the heaviest biology chapter of Class 10 and almost always brings a diagram question, a 'differences in tabular form' question and one long answer on the heart, the digestive system or the kidney.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 10 Science is one 80-mark paper in which the three biology chapters (Life Processes, Control and Coordination, How do Organisms Reproduce?) together with Heredity sit inside the unit 'World of Living', which carries about 25 marks. Life Processes is the longest chapter in that unit and typically contributes 6 to 8 marks, spread over an MCQ or assertion-reason item, a 2 or 3 mark question and often a 5 mark question or a 4 mark case study.

question_types.note: Site of a process (where pyruvate is broken down, where fats are digested), the correct sequence of the digestive or respiratory passage, which vertebrate group has a two- or three-chambered heart, what opens and closes stomata, functions of xylem and phloem.

One statement about a structure and one about its function: ventricles thicker than atria, veins have valves, capillaries one cell thick, bile has no enzyme but is essential, glucose is reabsorbed in the nephron.

Two differences (arteries and veins, aerobic and anaerobic, autotrophic and heterotrophic), a reason (why diffusion is not enough, why aquatic animals breathe faster), role of saliva or HCl, functions of lymph or platelets.

Digestion of a food component step by step, double circulation and why it is needed, three events of photosynthesis, flow chart of glucose breakdown, transport of water in plants, comparison of alveoli and nephron, urine formation.
A labelled diagram (heart, alimentary canal, excretory system, respiratory system, nephron, stomata) with 2 or 3 sub-parts: functions of labelled parts, reasons, and one differences table.

A short passage on the photosynthesis experiments (KOH, variegated leaf), on dialysis and the artificial kidney, on the heart and blood pressure, or on respiration in yeast and in muscles, followed by four sub-questions.

hot_topics: Human digestive system: role of each organ, enzyme and gland, with the labelled diagram
Human heart, double circulation and why oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept apart
Aerobic and anaerobic respiration: flow chart of glucose breakdown, differences in tabular form
Photosynthesis: the equation, the three events, stomata and guard cells, the experiments
Excretion in humans: nephron structure, urine formation, artificial kidney
Arteries, veins and capillaries; blood, platelets and lymph
Transport of water (transpiration pull) and food (translocation) in plants
Alveoli and nephron compared; how lungs are designed to maximise gas exchange

sections.heading: 5.1 What are Life Processes?
sections.body:
The chapter opens with a simple question: how do we decide that something is alive? Visible movement is not a safe test, because a sleeping dog or a plant does not move in any obvious way, yet both are alive. What is common to all living things is that they are organised systems whose structures keep breaking down and must be repaired, so every living thing needs a steady supply of energy and building material even when it seems to be doing nothing. The processes that do this maintenance work are called life processes.

NCERT names four of them and the chapter is built around them:

  • Nutrition: taking in energy and material from outside. Autotrophs like green plants make their food from carbon dioxide and water; heterotrophs like animals and fungi take ready-made food from other organisms.
  • Respiration: breaking down the food inside cells to release energy, usually by oxidation with oxygen taken in from outside.
  • Transportation: carrying food, oxygen and wastes from where they are taken in or made to every cell of the body.
  • Excretion: removing the harmful by-products of metabolism.

The key idea the examiner looks for is the link between body size and the need for organ systems. In a unicellular organism such as Amoeba, the whole surface of the cell touches the environment, so diffusion is enough to bring in food and oxygen and to throw out wastes. In a multicellular organism most cells are far from the surface, and diffusion is far too slow to supply every cell, so specialised tissues and organs (gut, lungs, heart, kidneys) take over each function. Write this reason whenever you are asked why humans need a respiratory or circulatory system.
sections.tip: If a question asks 'why do multicellular organisms need special organs for exchange of gases', the one-line marking point is: diffusion is too slow to reach every cell because most cells are not in direct contact with the surroundings.

sections.heading: 5.2 Nutrition and 5.2.1 Autotrophic Nutrition
sections.body:
Food supplies two things: energy, and the carbon-based material from which the body is built and repaired. Depending on how the carbon is obtained, nutrition is autotrophic (organism makes complex organic food from CO2 and water, using light energy) or heterotrophic (organism takes complex organic food made by others).

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and some bacteria carry out autotrophic nutrition. NCERT writes it as:

6CO2 + 12H2O → (sunlight, chlorophyll) → C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O

Three events occur, and boards ask for them by name and in order:

  1. Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll.
  2. Conversion of light energy to chemical energy, and splitting of water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen.
  3. Reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates.

The steps need not happen one after the other. Desert plants take up CO2 at night and store it as an intermediate, then use light energy during the day to reduce it, because their stomata stay closed in the daytime to save water. Carbohydrate not used at once is stored as starch, the plant's internal energy reserve, just as animals store glycogen.

Where does a plant get its raw materials? Water and minerals come from the soil through the roots. CO2 enters through the stomata, tiny pores on the leaf surface guarded by a pair of guard cells. When water flows into the guard cells they swell and the pore opens; when they lose water they shrink and the pore closes. Since a lot of water is lost through open stomata, the plant opens them only when it needs CO2. Nitrogen for making proteins is not taken from the air directly; it is absorbed as inorganic nitrates and nitrites from the soil, or as organic compounds made by bacteria from atmospheric nitrogen.

Two NCERT activities and one standard experiment are exam favourites. (i) The variegated leaf (money plant or Croton): the plant is kept in the dark for three days to destarch it, then in sunlight for six hours; the leaf is boiled in water, then in alcohol over a water bath to remove chlorophyll, and tested with iodine. Only the green parts turn blue-black, proving chlorophyll is essential. (ii) Two destarched potted plants under bell jars, one with a watch glass of KOH, which absorbs CO2; only the leaf from the plant without KOH tests positive for starch, proving CO2 is essential. (iii) Covering part of a leaf with black paper before exposing it to light shows that sunlight is essential.

where: released from the splitting of water, not from CO<sub>2</sub>

sections.tip: Write 'sunlight' and 'chlorophyll' above the arrow. Leaving them out loses the equation mark even if the formulae are right.

sections.heading: 5.2.2 Heterotrophic Nutrition
sections.body:
Heterotrophs cannot make their own food and depend directly or indirectly on autotrophs. The form of nutrition depends on the type of food and how it is obtained, and NCERT describes three strategies. You should be able to define each and give two examples.

  • Saprophytic nutrition: the organism secretes digestive enzymes on to dead and decaying organic matter outside its body, breaks it down there and then absorbs the simple soluble products. Examples: fungi such as bread moulds, yeast and mushrooms, and many bacteria.
  • Parasitic nutrition: the organism lives on or inside another living organism (the host) and derives nutrition from it without killing it, usually harming it. Examples: Cuscuta (amarbel) on plants, ticks, lice, leeches and tapeworms on animals.
  • Holozoic nutrition: the organism takes in whole food, complex or solid, and breaks it down inside the body. This is the mode of most animals, including humans, Amoeba and Paramoecium. The steps are ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion.

Note the wording in the examiner's answer key. Saprophytes digest outside the body and absorb; holozoic organisms digest inside the body. Parasites take food from a living host; saprophytes from dead matter. A frequent 2-mark question asks for two differences between holozoic and saprophytic nutrition, so keep these two contrasts ready in tabular form.

The chapter also makes a general point: since the food of a heterotroph is complex, it must be broken down into simpler substances before it can be absorbed and used. This breaking down is done by enzymes, biocatalysts that convert complex food into simple, soluble molecules. Different organisms use different enzymes depending on the food they eat and the way they obtain it.
sections.tip: When asked to name a parasitic plant, write Cuscuta (amarbel). Students often write 'mushroom', which is a saprophyte, and lose the mark.

sections.heading: 5.2.3 How do Organisms obtain their Nutrition?
sections.body:
In a single-celled organism the whole surface is in contact with the environment, so food can be taken in over the entire surface. As organisms grow larger and more complex, different parts specialise for different steps of nutrition.

Nutrition in Amoeba is the NCERT example and a regular diagram question. Amoeba takes in food using temporary finger-like extensions of the cell surface called pseudopodia. The pseudopodia fuse over the food particle and enclose it in a food vacuole. Inside the food vacuole, enzymes break the complex food into simpler substances, which then diffuse into the cytoplasm. The undigested material is moved to the surface of the cell and thrown out. This is holozoic nutrition in a single cell: ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion all happen in one cell.

Nutrition in Paramoecium is different because the cell has a definite shape. Food is taken in only at a specific spot, and it is moved to that spot by the movement of cilia, the tiny hair-like structures that cover the entire surface of the cell.

The point the examiner wants is the contrast: Amoeba can take in food at any point on its surface using pseudopodia, while Paramoecium takes food only at a fixed spot with the help of cilia. Pseudopodia also serve Amoeba for locomotion, which is the usual second purpose asked in a diagram question.

For the diagram, draw an irregular cell outline, a nucleus, one or two pseudopodia curving round a food particle, and a food vacuole inside the cytoplasm. Label pseudopodia, food particle, food vacuole and nucleus. Show the stages as three or four small sketches if the question says 'show the steps of nutrition'.
sections.tip: Spell them as NCERT does: Amoeba, Paramoecium, pseudopodia, cilia. Spelling is not penalised heavily but a correctly named 'food vacuole' is one of the labelling marks.

sections.heading: 5.2.4 Nutrition in Human Beings
sections.body:
The alimentary canal is a long tube from the mouth to the anus, and different parts of it are specialised for different functions. Learn the passage in order: mouth (buccal cavity) → oesophagus (food pipe) → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus.

Mouth. Teeth crush the food and the tongue mixes it with saliva, secreted by the salivary glands. Saliva wets the food so it can be swallowed, and its enzyme salivary amylase breaks starch (a complex carbohydrate) into simple sugar. That is why bread tastes sweet when chewed for a while. The lining of the canal has muscles that contract rhythmically to push food along; this peristaltic movement occurs all along the gut.

Stomach. The muscular walls mix the food with gastric juice from the gastric glands, which contains three things: hydrochloric acid (creates an acidic medium so that pepsin can act, and kills bacteria), pepsin (a protein-digesting enzyme) and mucus (protects the stomach lining from the acid). The exit of the stomach is controlled by a sphincter muscle that releases food in small amounts into the small intestine.

Small intestine. This is the longest part of the canal and the site of complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Its length depends on the diet: herbivores like cows have a longer small intestine to digest cellulose, while carnivores like tigers have a shorter one because meat is easier to digest. Food arriving from the stomach is acidic; bile juice from the liver makes it alkaline so the pancreatic enzymes can act. Bile contains no enzyme, but its salts emulsify fats, breaking large globules into tiny droplets that give the enzyme more surface to act on. The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice containing trypsin (digests proteins) and lipase (breaks down emulsified fats). Glands in the intestinal wall secrete intestinal juice, which finally converts proteins to amino acids, complex carbohydrates to glucose and fats to fatty acids and glycerol.

The inner lining of the small intestine has many finger-like projections called villi, which increase the surface area for absorption; they are richly supplied with blood vessels that take the absorbed food to every cell for building new tissue, repairing old tissue and providing energy. Unabsorbed food passes to the large intestine, where more water is absorbed, and the rest is removed through the anus under the control of the anal sphincter.
sections.tip: The most repeated 5-marker is 'explain digestion in mouth, stomach and small intestine'. Marking points: salivary amylase and starch; HCl, pepsin and mucus; bile emulsifies; trypsin and lipase; end products; villi. Write all six.

sections.heading: 5.3 Respiration: the breakdown of glucose
sections.body:
Digested food is used as a source of energy inside cells. The food is broken down by oxidation, and this whole process is called respiration. Note the difference the examiner insists on: breathing is the physical process of taking in oxygen and giving out CO2; respiration is the chemical breakdown of food in cells to release energy.

The first step, common to all organisms, is the breakdown of glucose (a six-carbon molecule) into pyruvate (a three-carbon molecule) in the cytoplasm. What happens to pyruvate next depends on whether oxygen is available, and NCERT gives three pathways. Learn them as a flow chart because it is asked for exactly that way:

  • Absence of oxygen (in yeast during fermentation): pyruvate → ethanol + CO2 + energy. This is anaerobic respiration.
  • Lack of oxygen (in our muscle cells during sudden, vigorous activity): pyruvate → lactic acid + energy. The build-up of lactic acid causes muscle cramps.
  • Presence of oxygen (in mitochondria): pyruvate → CO2 + water + energy. This is aerobic respiration and releases much more energy than the anaerobic pathways.

The energy released is used at once to make ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. ATP is the energy currency of the cell: when the terminal phosphate bond is broken, about 30.5 kJ/mol of energy is released, and this drives muscle contraction, protein synthesis, conduction of nerve impulses and every other activity of the cell.

For the tabular differences question, the standard three rows are: aerobic needs oxygen while anaerobic does not; aerobic occurs in cytoplasm and mitochondria while anaerobic occurs only in the cytoplasm; aerobic gives CO2 and water and much more energy while anaerobic gives ethanol and CO2 (or lactic acid) and much less energy. Examples of organisms using anaerobic respiration: yeast, some bacteria.

Plants exchange gases through stomata and the large intercellular spaces, by diffusion. The direction of diffusion depends on the environment and the need of the plant: at night, when there is no photosynthesis, CO2 is given out; during the day, the CO2 from respiration is used up in photosynthesis and oxygen is the major gas released.

formulas.expr: Glucose (6C) → pyruvate (3C) + energy, in the cytoplasm
where: three-carbon molecule; common first step in all organisms

formulas.expr: Pyruvate → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + energy (presence of O<sub>2</sub>, in mitochondria)
where: site of aerobic breakdown, hence 'powerhouse of the cell'

formulas.expr: Pyruvate → ethanol + CO<sub>2</sub> + energy (absence of O<sub>2</sub>, yeast); pyruvate → lactic acid + energy (lack of O<sub>2</sub>, muscles)
where: its accumulation in muscles causes cramps

sections.tip: The MCQ trap: glucose to pyruvate happens in the cytoplasm; only the further breakdown of pyruvate with oxygen happens in the mitochondria.

sections.heading: 5.3 Respiration: exchange of gases in animals and in human beings
sections.body:
Since aerobic respiration needs a continuous supply of oxygen, organisms need a way to take in oxygen and throw out CO2. Aquatic animals use oxygen dissolved in water, which is far less than the oxygen in air, so they breathe much faster. Fish take in water through the mouth and force it past the gills, where oxygen is taken up by blood. Terrestrial animals take oxygen from the air, and the respiratory organs of all animals share three features: a large surface area, a fine and delicate surface, and a rich blood supply (in animals that transport gases in blood).

The human respiratory system. Air enters through the nostrils; fine hairs and mucus in the nasal passage filter out dust. It passes through the throat (pharynx), then the larynx and the trachea, which is held open by rings of cartilage so that the air passage does not collapse. In the chest the trachea divides into two bronchi, one to each lung, which divide into smaller and smaller bronchioles, ending in balloon-like alveoli. The alveoli provide an enormous surface for gas exchange, about 80 m2 in a human, and their walls carry an extensive network of blood capillaries.

Breathing. When we breathe in, the ribs are lifted and the diaphragm flattens, so the chest cavity becomes larger and air is drawn into the lungs and fills the alveoli. Blood brings CO2 from the body to the alveoli for release, and takes up oxygen from the alveolar air. During the breathing cycle the lungs always retain a residual volume of air, so there is enough time for oxygen to be absorbed and CO2 to be released.

Transport of gases. Oxygen has low solubility in water, so it is carried by the respiratory pigment haemoglobin in the red blood cells, which has a high affinity for oxygen. CO2 is more soluble in water and is mostly transported in dissolved form in the blood plasma. A deficiency of haemoglobin means less oxygen reaches the tissues, producing weakness and breathlessness (anaemia).

Diffusion would be enough for a small animal, but in a large body it would take years for oxygen to reach the deepest cells; a circulatory system is therefore needed to carry the gases, which is the link to the next section.
sections.tip: For 'how are lungs designed to maximise gas exchange' give three points: alveoli are very many, so the surface area is large (about 80 m²); their walls are thin; they are surrounded by a network of capillaries.

sections.heading: 5.4.1 Transportation in Human Beings: blood, the heart and double circulation
sections.body:
Blood is a fluid connective tissue. The fluid part, plasma, carries food, CO2 and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form; the red blood cells carry oxygen, and the blood also carries salts and other substances. Blood needs a pumping organ, a network of tubes to reach every tissue, and a system to repair the network if it leaks.

The heart is a muscular organ about the size of a fist, with four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. Because both oxygen and CO2 travel in blood, the heart is built so that oxygen-rich blood does not mix with CO2-rich blood. Follow the path, since a diagram question usually asks you to label 'the chamber that...':

  1. Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium (through the pulmonary veins) while it relaxes.
  2. The left atrium contracts and the blood passes into the left ventricle, which relaxes to receive it.
  3. The left ventricle contracts and pumps blood to the whole body through the aorta.
  4. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium (through the vena cava) as it relaxes.
  5. The right atrium contracts and the blood enters the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs through the pulmonary artery to pick up oxygen.

The ventricles pump blood into organs, so they have thicker muscular walls than the atria. Valves between atria and ventricles and at the base of the great vessels ensure that blood does not flow backwards when the chambers contract. A muscular wall, the septum, separates the right and left sides.

Double circulation. Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle: once from body to heart to lungs (pulmonary circulation), and once from lungs to heart to body (systemic circulation). The separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood allows a highly efficient supply of oxygen, which birds and mammals need because they use energy constantly to keep their body temperature constant. Amphibians and reptiles have three-chambered hearts and tolerate some mixing; fish have two-chambered hearts, blood is pumped to the gills, oxygenated there and sent directly to the body, so it goes through the heart only once per cycle.

The force with which blood pushes against the wall of an artery is blood pressure: about 120 mm of Hg during ventricular contraction (systolic) and 80 mm of Hg during relaxation (diastolic), measured with a sphygmomanometer. High blood pressure (hypertension) is caused by constriction of arterioles and can rupture an artery.
sections.tip: In the heart diagram the left side of the heart is drawn on the right of the page. Label pulmonary artery leaving the right ventricle and aorta leaving the left ventricle; swapping them is the most common labelling error.

sections.heading: 5.4.1 Transportation in Human Beings: blood vessels, platelets and lymph
sections.body:
Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the organs. Because blood leaves the heart under high pressure, arteries have thick, elastic walls. Veins collect blood from the organs and bring it back to the heart. Blood in veins is under low pressure, so they have thinner walls, and they have valves that make sure blood flows in only one direction. On reaching an organ, an artery divides into smaller and smaller vessels until it forms capillaries, whose walls are only one cell thick so that materials can be exchanged between the blood and the surrounding cells. Capillaries join up to form veins that carry the blood away from the organ.

For the standard differences table: arteries carry blood from the heart, veins to the heart; arteries carry oxygenated blood (except the pulmonary artery), veins carry deoxygenated blood (except the pulmonary vein); arteries have thick elastic walls and no valves, veins have thin walls and valves; blood flows under high pressure in arteries and low pressure in veins.

Maintenance by platelets. Any leak in the system reduces the pressure and the efficiency of pumping. The blood has platelet cells, which circulate around the body and plug leaks by helping to clot the blood at the points of injury.

Lymph. Through the pores in the walls of capillaries some plasma, proteins and blood cells escape into the spaces between cells and form tissue fluid or lymph. It is similar to plasma but colourless and contains less protein. Lymph drains into lymphatic capillaries, which join to form larger lymph vessels that finally open into the larger veins. Two functions you must know: lymph carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine, and it drains excess fluid from the extracellular space back into the blood.

A frequent 3-mark question asks for the function of each component of the human transport system: heart (pumps blood), blood (carries O2, food, CO2, wastes), blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries as routes), platelets (clotting), lymph (fat transport and drainage). Write one line for each.
sections.tip: Write the exceptions in the arteries versus veins table: pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood. Examiners reward it and it protects you from an MCQ on the same point.

sections.heading: 5.4.2 Transportation in Plants
sections.body:
Plants are large and their two ends do different jobs: roots take in water and minerals from the soil, leaves make food. Diffusion between neighbouring cells is far too slow to carry raw materials to the leaves and food to the roots, so plants have a transport system made of two conducting tissues: xylem for water and minerals, phloem for the products of photosynthesis. Plants have low energy needs because they do not move, so they can use a slow transport system.

Transport of water. In xylem the vessels and tracheids of roots, stems and leaves are interconnected to form a continuous system of water-conducting channels. Root cells actively take up ions from the soil, which creates a difference in ion concentration between the root and the soil; water moves into the root to balance it, and a steady column of water is pushed upwards. This root pressure is enough for small plants, but not to lift water to the top of a tall tree. There the main force is transpiration pull: water evaporates from the leaf cells through the stomata, creating a suction that pulls water up from the xylem of the roots. So root pressure is important at night, when stomata are closed, and transpiration pull is the major driver during the day.

Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of the plant. It (i) helps in the absorption and upward movement of water and dissolved minerals, and (ii) helps in temperature regulation by cooling the leaf. This is the standard answer to 'give three reasons why transpiration is important'.

Transport of food and other substances. The movement of soluble products of photosynthesis through phloem is called translocation. Phloem also carries amino acids and other substances, and delivers them to roots, fruits, seeds and growing organs. Unlike transport in xylem, translocation needs energy. Sucrose is loaded into the phloem tissue (sieve tubes with companion cells) using energy from ATP; this raises the osmotic pressure, water moves in, and the pressure pushes the material to tissues where the pressure is lower. Because this pressure is adjustable, phloem can move material up or down according to the plant's needs, for example carrying sugar stored in the roots up to the buds in spring.

For the differences table: xylem moves water and minerals upwards only from roots to leaves, needs no energy, uses physical forces (transpiration pull); phloem moves food and amino acids in both directions, from leaves to storage organs and back, and uses ATP.
sections.tip: The 2-mark reason question: at night, when there is no transpiration, water still moves up because of root pressure. Students who write 'transpiration' for night time lose both marks.

sections.heading: 5.5.1 Excretion in Human Beings
sections.body:
Excretion is the biological process of removing harmful metabolic wastes from the body. Unicellular organisms remove wastes by simple diffusion into the surrounding water; complex multicellular organisms use specialised organs. In humans the excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra. Urine produced in the kidneys passes through the ureters into the bladder, where it is stored until it is released through the urethra.

How is urine produced? The purpose of making urine is to filter out waste products from the blood. Just as CO2 is removed in the lungs, nitrogenous wastes such as urea and uric acid are removed from blood in the kidneys. Each kidney contains a very large number of filtration units called nephrons, packed close together. In a nephron, blood from the renal artery enters a cluster of very thin-walled capillaries, the glomerulus, which sits inside a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule. Water and dissolved substances are filtered from the glomerulus into the capsule under pressure. The filtrate then flows along the long coiled tubule of the nephron, where useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water are selectively reabsorbed into the blood. The amount of water reabsorbed depends on how much excess water there is in the body and on how much dissolved waste has to be excreted. The urine that remains drains into the collecting duct and then into the ureter.

The bladder is muscular and under nervous control, so we can usually control the urge to urinate. Since a large volume of filtrate is produced but only about 1.5 litres of urine leave the body each day, the tubule's reabsorption is the key to answering 'why is the volume of urine so much less than the filtrate'.

Artificial kidney (haemodialysis). Kidneys can fail because of infection, injury or restricted blood flow. In dialysis the patient's blood is passed through a series of tubes made of a semi-permeable membrane, suspended in a tank of dialysing fluid whose osmotic pressure is the same as blood but without the nitrogenous wastes. Wastes diffuse from the blood into the fluid, and the cleaned blood is returned to the patient. The function is similar to the kidney, but there is no reabsorption, which is the difference the examiner looks for.
sections.tip: For the nephron diagram label Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, tubule, collecting duct and the renal artery and vein. Always draw the glomerulus inside the capsule, not beside it.

sections.heading: 5.5.2 Excretion in Plants
sections.body:
Plants use completely different strategies for excretion from animals, and a 3-mark question regularly asks you to 'list four strategies used by plants for excretion'. Plants do not have organs like kidneys, so they manage their wastes in several simple ways.

  • Gaseous wastes. Oxygen is a waste product of photosynthesis and carbon dioxide of respiration. They are removed through the stomata and lenticels by diffusion, and since each is used up by the other process during the day, the net exchange depends on the time of day.
  • Excess water is removed by transpiration through the stomata.
  • Storage in cellular vacuoles. Many plant waste products are stored in the vacuoles of cells, where they do no harm.
  • Storage in leaves that fall off. Wastes are moved into old leaves, which are then shed; shedding leaves is a way of getting rid of accumulated waste.
  • Resins and gums. Other wastes are stored as resins and gums, especially in old xylem that no longer conducts water.
  • Excretion into the soil. Some waste substances are excreted directly into the soil around the plant through the roots.

The idea worth stating in any answer is that many plant wastes are removed very slowly, because plants have a low rate of metabolism compared with animals and can afford to store wastes for long periods. Notice that the same structures do double duty: stomata release oxygen and water vapour and take in CO2, and the old xylem that transported water becomes a dump for resins. Two of these examples with the phrase 'stored in' or 'removed through' earns the full three marks.
sections.tip: If asked to name two excretory products in plants other than O₂ and CO₂, write resins and gums (or tannins, latex); do not write 'urea', which plants do not produce as a waste.

key_terms.definition: The basic functions performed by living organisms to maintain their life: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion.
Mode of nutrition in which an organism makes its own complex organic food from simple inorganic substances (CO₂ and water) using sunlight and chlorophyll, as in green plants.
Mode of nutrition in which an organism takes ready-made complex organic food from other organisms; may be saprophytic, parasitic or holozoic.
The process by which green plants make carbohydrates from CO₂ and water using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll, releasing oxygen.
Tiny pores on the surface of leaves, each bounded by two guard cells, through which gas exchange and transpiration occur; they open when the guard cells swell with water.
Nutrition in which digestive enzymes are secreted on dead organic matter outside the body and the digested products are absorbed, as in fungi such as bread mould and mushrooms.
Nutrition in which an organism derives food from another living organism (host) without killing it, as in Cuscuta, ticks, lice and tapeworms.
Nutrition in which whole food is taken in and broken down inside the body, involving ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion, as in Amoeba and humans.
Rhythmic contraction of the muscles of the alimentary canal that pushes food along the gut.
Breaking of large fat globules into tiny droplets by bile salts in the small intestine, increasing the surface area on which lipase can act.
Numerous finger-like projections on the inner lining of the small intestine that increase the surface area for absorption of digested food and are richly supplied with blood vessels.
The process in which food is broken down by oxidation inside cells to release energy; it may be aerobic (with oxygen) or anaerobic (without oxygen).

Adenosine triphosphate, the energy currency of the cell; energy released in respiration is used to make ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate, and about 30.5 kJ/mol is released when its terminal phosphate bond is broken.
Balloon-like structures at the ends of the bronchioles in the lungs whose thin walls, large total surface area and rich capillary supply make them the site of gas exchange.
The respiratory pigment in red blood cells that has a high affinity for oxygen and carries it from the lungs to the tissues.
Circulation in which blood passes through the heart twice in each complete cycle, once to the lungs and once to the rest of the body, keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.
Colourless tissue fluid formed from plasma, proteins and blood cells that escape through capillary walls; it carries absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid back into the blood.
Loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata; it creates the suction (transpiration pull) that draws water up the xylem and helps cool the plant.
Transport of soluble products of photosynthesis and other substances through phloem from leaves to other parts of the plant; it requires energy from ATP and can occur in both directions.
The biological process by which harmful metabolic wastes are removed from the body.

The structural and functional unit of the kidney, consisting of Bowman's capsule enclosing a glomerulus, a long coiled tubule and a collecting duct, in which urine is formed by filtration and selective reabsorption.
Removal of nitrogenous wastes from blood by an artificial kidney in which blood flows through semi-permeable tubes suspended in dialysing fluid; unlike the kidney it involves no reabsorption.

formula_sheet.name: Photosynthesis equation
formula_sheet.note: Write 'sunlight' and 'chlorophyll' above the arrow; oxygen comes from the splitting of water.

formula_sheet.name: Three events of photosynthesis
formula_sheet.expr: absorption of light by chlorophyll → conversion of light energy to chemical energy and splitting of water → reduction of CO<sub>2</sub> to carbohydrates
formula_sheet.note: State them in this order in a 3-mark answer.

formula_sheet.name: Glycolysis (first step of respiration)
formula_sheet.note: Occurs in the cytoplasm of all organisms, with or without oxygen.

formula_sheet.name: Aerobic respiration
formula_sheet.expr: Pyruvate → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + energy (in mitochondria, in presence of O<sub>2</sub>)
formula_sheet.note: Releases much more energy than anaerobic pathways.

formula_sheet.name: Anaerobic respiration
formula_sheet.expr: Pyruvate → ethanol + CO<sub>2</sub> + energy (yeast); pyruvate → lactic acid + energy (muscle, lack of O<sub>2</sub>)
formula_sheet.note: Lactic acid build-up causes cramps; both occur in the cytoplasm.

formula_sheet.name: ATP energy
formula_sheet.expr: ATP → ADP + inorganic phosphate + about 30.5 kJ/mol
formula_sheet.note: ATP is the energy currency for most cellular processes.

formula_sheet.name: Alveolar surface area
formula_sheet.note: The number to quote when explaining how lungs maximise gas exchange.

formula_sheet.name: Normal blood pressure
formula_sheet.expr: systolic about 120 mm Hg; diastolic about 80 mm Hg
formula_sheet.note: Measured with a sphygmomanometer; hypertension results from constriction of arterioles.

formula_sheet.name: Heart chambers across vertebrates
formula_sheet.expr: fish 2 chambers (single circulation); amphibians and reptiles 3 chambers (some mixing); birds and mammals 4 chambers (double circulation)
formula_sheet.note: Warm-blooded animals need full separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

formula_sheet.name: End products of digestion
formula_sheet.expr: carbohydrates → glucose; proteins → amino acids; fats → fatty acids + glycerol
formula_sheet.note: All three are completed in the small intestine.

formula_sheet.name: Urine output
formula_sheet.expr: about 1.5 litres of urine per day from a very much larger volume of glomerular filtrate
formula_sheet.note: The difference is the water and useful substances reabsorbed in the tubule.

Show the nucleus and cytoplasm in each. Label pseudopodia, food particle, food vacuole and nucleus.

ncert_questions.q: Why is diffusion insufficient to meet the oxygen requirements of multicellular organisms like humans?
ncert_questions.a: In a multicellular organism the body is large and most of its cells are not in direct contact with the surrounding environment. Diffusion is a very slow process, so if oxygen had to reach the deepest cells by diffusion alone it would take an extremely long time and the cells would die for want of oxygen. Multicellular organisms therefore need a specialised respiratory system to take in oxygen and a circulatory system to carry it rapidly to every cell.

ncert_questions.q: What criteria do we use to decide whether something is alive?
ncert_questions.a: Visible movement is not a reliable criterion, since a sleeping animal or a plant may show no obvious movement yet be alive. The criterion we use is that living things maintain themselves: they show molecular movement, they repair and maintain their organised structures, and they carry out the life processes of nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion. Growth and the ability to respond to the environment are further signs.

ncert_questions.q: What processes would you consider essential for maintaining life?
ncert_questions.a: Nutrition (obtaining energy and material from outside), respiration (breaking down food inside cells to release energy), transportation (carrying food, oxygen and wastes to and from every cell) and excretion (removing harmful metabolic wastes). These four are the maintenance processes; even an organism at rest needs them to keep its structures intact.

ncert_questions.q: What are the differences between autotrophic nutrition and heterotrophic nutrition?
ncert_questions.a: Autotrophic nutrition: the organism makes its own food from simple inorganic substances (CO2 and water) using light energy and chlorophyll; it does not depend on other organisms for food; examples are green plants and some bacteria. Heterotrophic nutrition: the organism cannot make its own food and takes ready-made complex organic food from other organisms, directly or indirectly; chlorophyll is absent; examples are animals, fungi and most bacteria.

ncert_questions.q: What is the role of the acid in our stomach?
ncert_questions.a: Hydrochloric acid secreted by the gastric glands (i) creates an acidic medium in the stomach, which is necessary for the enzyme pepsin to act on proteins, and (ii) kills harmful bacteria and other microorganisms that enter with food.

ncert_questions.q: How is the small intestine designed to absorb digested food?
ncert_questions.a: The small intestine is very long, so food stays in it long enough to be completely digested and absorbed. Its inner lining has numerous finger-like projections called villi, which greatly increase the surface area for absorption. The villi are richly supplied with blood vessels, which carry the absorbed food to every cell of the body for building and repairing tissues and for energy.

ncert_questions.q: What advantage over an aquatic organism does a terrestrial organism have with regard to obtaining oxygen for respiration?
ncert_questions.a: A terrestrial organism takes oxygen from the air, where its concentration is much higher than the amount of oxygen dissolved in water. An aquatic organism has to move water past its gills continuously and breathe much faster to obtain enough oxygen. The terrestrial organism therefore obtains oxygen with less effort and can support a higher rate of respiration.

ncert_questions.q: How are the oxygen and carbon dioxide transported in human beings?
ncert_questions.a: Oxygen is poorly soluble in water, so it is carried by the respiratory pigment haemoglobin present in the red blood cells. Haemoglobin has a high affinity for oxygen, picks it up in the alveoli of the lungs and releases it in the tissues. Carbon dioxide is more soluble in water and is transported mainly in dissolved form in the blood plasma from the tissues to the lungs, where it is released into the alveoli.

ncert_questions.q: Why is it necessary to separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in mammals and birds?
ncert_questions.a: Mammals and birds are warm-blooded: they use energy continuously to keep their body temperature constant, so they have a very high energy need. Keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate allows a highly efficient supply of oxygen to the body, because oxygen-rich blood from the lungs is not diluted by carbon dioxide-rich blood from the body before it is pumped to the tissues.

ncert_questions.q: The kidneys in human beings are a part of the system for (a) nutrition (b) respiration (c) excretion (d) transportation.
ncert_questions.a: (c) excretion. The kidneys filter nitrogenous wastes such as urea from the blood and form urine.

ncert_questions.q: The xylem in plants are responsible for (a) transport of water (b) transport of food (c) transport of amino acids (d) transport of oxygen.
ncert_questions.a: (a) transport of water. Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves; food and amino acids are carried by phloem.

ncert_questions.q: The autotrophic mode of nutrition requires (a) carbon dioxide and water (b) chlorophyll (c) sunlight (d) all of the above.
ncert_questions.a: (d) all of the above. Photosynthesis needs CO2 and water as raw materials, chlorophyll to absorb light and sunlight as the source of energy.

ncert_questions.q: The breakdown of pyruvate to give carbon dioxide, water and energy takes place in (a) cytoplasm (b) mitochondria (c) chloroplast (d) nucleus.
ncert_questions.a: (b) mitochondria. Glucose is first broken into pyruvate in the cytoplasm; the aerobic breakdown of pyruvate into CO2, water and energy occurs in the mitochondria.

ncert_questions.q: How are fats digested in our bodies? Where does this process take place?
ncert_questions.a: Fats are digested in the small intestine. Fat enters the intestine from the stomach as large globules, which are difficult for enzymes to act upon. Bile juice from the liver, stored in the gall bladder, contains bile salts that emulsify the fat, breaking the globules into tiny droplets and increasing the surface area for enzyme action. Bile also makes the acidic food alkaline so that pancreatic enzymes can work. The enzyme lipase in pancreatic juice then breaks down the emulsified fat, and intestinal juice completes the conversion of fats into fatty acids and glycerol, which are absorbed by the villi.

ncert_questions.q: What is the role of saliva in the digestion of food?
ncert_questions.a: Saliva, secreted by the salivary glands, (i) moistens the food so that it can be chewed, mixed and swallowed easily, and (ii) contains the enzyme salivary amylase, which breaks down starch (a complex carbohydrate) into simple sugars, so the digestion of carbohydrates begins in the mouth.

ncert_questions.q: What are the necessary conditions for autotrophic nutrition and what are its by-products?
ncert_questions.a: Conditions: (i) presence of chlorophyll to absorb light energy, (ii) sunlight as the energy source, (iii) carbon dioxide from the air taken in through stomata, and (iv) water absorbed from the soil by the roots. By-products: oxygen, released through the stomata, and water. The carbohydrate formed is stored as starch.

ncert_questions.q: What are the differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration? Name some organisms that use the anaerobic mode of respiration.
ncert_questions.a: Aerobic respiration: takes place in the presence of oxygen; glucose is completely broken down into CO2 and water; occurs in the cytoplasm (glucose to pyruvate) and then in the mitochondria; releases a large amount of energy. Anaerobic respiration: takes place in the absence of oxygen; glucose is incompletely broken down into ethanol and CO2 (or lactic acid); occurs entirely in the cytoplasm; releases much less energy. Organisms using anaerobic respiration: yeast (during fermentation) and some bacteria; our muscle cells also respire anaerobically for a short time when oxygen is lacking.

ncert_questions.q: How are the alveoli designed to maximise the exchange of gases?
ncert_questions.a: (i) The alveoli are very numerous, so together they provide a very large surface area, about 80 m2 in a human, for the exchange of gases. (ii) Their walls are very thin, so gases diffuse through them easily. (iii) The walls of the alveoli are surrounded by an extensive network of blood capillaries, so oxygen is taken up and CO2 released quickly.

ncert_questions.q: What would be the consequences of a deficiency of haemoglobin in our bodies?
ncert_questions.a: Haemoglobin in the red blood cells carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. If haemoglobin is deficient, less oxygen reaches the cells, so less energy is released by aerobic respiration. The person feels weak and tired, becomes breathless on slight exertion and looks pale. This condition is called anaemia.

ncert_questions.q: Describe double circulation in human beings. Why is it necessary?
ncert_questions.a: In human beings blood passes through the heart twice during one complete cycle, which is called double circulation. (i) Pulmonary circulation: deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the vena cava, passes into the right ventricle and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it gives up CO2 and takes up oxygen. (ii) Systemic circulation: oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle and is pumped through the aorta to all parts of the body. Valves prevent backflow, and the septum keeps the two sides apart. It is necessary because it keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood completely separate, giving a highly efficient supply of oxygen to the tissues, which humans need for their high energy demand and to maintain a constant body temperature.

ncert_questions.q: What are the differences between the transport of materials in xylem and phloem?
ncert_questions.a: Xylem: transports water and dissolved minerals; movement is only upward, from roots to leaves; driven by physical forces, root pressure and transpiration pull; does not require energy; conducted through vessels and tracheids, which are dead at maturity. Phloem: transports the soluble products of photosynthesis (sucrose) and amino acids; movement is in both directions, from leaves to storage organs and from storage organs to growing parts; needs energy from ATP to load sucrose; conducted through living sieve tubes with companion cells.

ncert_questions.q: Compare the functioning of alveoli in the lungs and nephrons in the kidneys with respect to their structures and functioning.
ncert_questions.a: Structure: alveoli are thin-walled, balloon-like sacs at the ends of the bronchioles, surrounded by a network of capillaries; nephrons are long coiled tubules, each beginning in a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule that encloses a knot of capillaries called the glomerulus. Both provide a very large surface area and a very thin surface, and both are closely associated with blood capillaries. Functioning: alveoli are the site of gas exchange: oxygen diffuses from the alveolar air into the blood and CO2 from the blood into the alveoli. Nephrons filter the blood: water and dissolved substances are filtered from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule, useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and water are selectively reabsorbed along the tubule, and the remaining urine is passed to the collecting duct. In short, alveoli remove a gaseous waste (CO2) while nephrons remove nitrogenous wastes dissolved in water.

pyq.q: The opening and closing of the stomatal pore depends upon:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: When water flows into the guard cells they swell and the pore opens; when they lose water they shrink and the pore closes.

pyq.q: In which of the following vertebrate group/groups, heart does not pump oxygenated blood to different parts of the body?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: In fishes the two-chambered heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills; the oxygenated blood then goes directly to the body without returning to the heart.

pyq.q: The breakdown of glucose into pyruvate takes place in the:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The first step of respiration, glucose to pyruvate, occurs in the cytoplasm of every cell; only the aerobic breakdown of pyruvate occurs in the mitochondria.

pyq.q: Which of the following is the correct sequence of parts in the human alimentary canal?
options: Mouth → stomach → small intestine → oesophagus → large intestine
Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → large intestine → small intestine
Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
Mouth → stomach → oesophagus → small intestine → large intestine
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Food passes from the mouth down the oesophagus into the stomach, then through the small intestine and finally the large intestine.

pyq.q: The enzyme secreted by the pancreas that digests proteins is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Pancreatic juice contains trypsin for proteins and lipase for fats; pepsin acts on proteins but is secreted by the gastric glands of the stomach.

pyq.q: Which of the following statements about lymph is correct?
options: It is red in colour and carries oxygen
It carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine
It contains more protein than blood plasma
It flows from the heart to the tissues
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Lymph is colourless, contains less protein than plasma, carries absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess tissue fluid into the veins.

pyq.q: In the experiment with two destarched potted plants under bell jars, a watch glass containing KOH is kept in one jar. The purpose of KOH is to:
options: absorb carbon dioxide from the air in the jar
supply carbon dioxide to the plant
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: KOH absorbs CO<sub>2</sub>; the plant in that jar cannot photosynthesise and its leaf gives a negative starch test, proving CO<sub>2</sub> is essential.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The walls of the ventricles are thicker than the walls of the atria. Reason (R): Ventricles have to pump blood into various organs of the body with great force.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Ventricles pump blood out of the heart to the lungs and the whole body, so they need thick muscular walls; atria only push blood into the ventricles.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Bile juice does not contain any digestive enzyme, yet it is essential for the digestion of fats. Reason (R): Bile salts emulsify fats, breaking large globules into tiny droplets so that lipase can act on a larger surface.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Both statements are NCERT facts and the emulsification explains why bile, though enzyme-free, is essential for fat digestion; bile also makes the acidic food alkaline for pancreatic enzymes.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Veins have valves in them. Reason (R): Blood in veins flows under high pressure.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Veins do have valves, but they are needed because blood in veins flows under low pressure and could flow backwards; it is arteries that carry blood under high pressure.

pyq.q: Why is diffusion insufficient to meet the oxygen requirements of large multicellular organisms like humans? What type of arrangement exists in the bodies of such animals to meet their oxygen requirement adequately?
pyq.answer:
(i) In a large multicellular body most cells are not in direct contact with the environment, and diffusion is a very slow process, so oxygen would take far too long to reach every cell.

(ii) Such animals have a specialised respiratory system (lungs with alveoli) to take in oxygen and a circulatory system (blood with haemoglobin pumped by the heart) to carry the oxygen rapidly to all cells.

pyq.q: State two differences between arteries and veins.
pyq.answer: Arteries: carry blood away from the heart to the organs; have thick, elastic walls because blood flows under high pressure; have no valves. Veins: carry blood from the organs back to the heart; have thin walls because blood flows under low pressure; have valves that prevent backflow. (Any two differences.)

pyq.q: What is the role of saliva in the digestion of food?
pyq.answer: (i) Saliva moistens and softens the food so that it can be chewed and swallowed easily. (ii) It contains the enzyme salivary amylase, which breaks down starch into simple sugar, so the digestion of complex carbohydrates begins in the mouth.

pyq.q: Name the two ways in which glucose is oxidised to provide energy in various organisms. Write one difference between them.
pyq.answer: Aerobic respiration and anaerobic respiration. Aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of oxygen and breaks glucose down completely into CO2 and water, releasing a large amount of energy; anaerobic respiration takes place in the absence of oxygen, breaks glucose down incompletely into ethanol and CO2 (or lactic acid) and releases much less energy.

pyq.q: (a) Why do the walls of the trachea not collapse when there is less air in it? (b) Why do aquatic animals breathe faster than terrestrial animals?
pyq.answer:
(a) The trachea is supported by rings of cartilage, which keep the air passage open even when there is little air in it.

(b) The amount of oxygen dissolved in water is much less than the amount of oxygen in air, so aquatic animals have to breathe faster to obtain enough oxygen.

pyq.q: (a) What do you mean by double circulation of blood? (b) Why is it necessary?
pyq.answer:
(a) In double circulation the blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium, goes to the right ventricle and is pumped to the lungs through the pulmonary artery (pulmonary circulation). Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium, goes to the left ventricle and is pumped to the whole body through the aorta (systemic circulation).

(b) It keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate, so the tissues receive a highly efficient supply of oxygen. This is necessary in mammals and birds, which have high energy needs because they constantly use energy to maintain a constant body temperature.

pyq.q: Compare alveoli in the lungs and nephrons in the kidneys with respect to their structure and functioning.
pyq.answer:
Structure: Alveoli are thin-walled, balloon-like sacs at the ends of bronchioles, very numerous, and surrounded by a network of capillaries. A nephron is a long coiled tubule starting in a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule that encloses a knot of capillaries, the glomerulus. Both have a large surface area, a thin surface and a rich blood supply.

Functioning: In alveoli, oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood and CO2 from the blood into the air, so alveoli exchange gases. In nephrons, water and dissolved substances are filtered from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule, useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts, water) are selectively reabsorbed along the tubule, and the urine left is sent to the collecting duct, so nephrons remove nitrogenous wastes.

pyq.q: With the help of a schematic flow chart, show the breakdown of glucose in a cell to provide energy (i) in the presence of oxygen, (ii) in the absence of oxygen, (iii) when there is lack of oxygen.
pyq.answer:
Glucose (6-carbon molecule) → in cytoplasm → pyruvate (3-carbon molecule) + energy. Then:

  • (i) Presence of oxygen (in mitochondria): pyruvate → CO2 + H2O + energy (aerobic respiration).
  • (ii) Absence of oxygen (in yeast): pyruvate → ethanol + CO2 + energy (fermentation).
  • (iii) Lack of oxygen (in our muscle cells): pyruvate → lactic acid + energy.

The energy released in each case is used to make ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.

pyq.q: 'About 180 litres of filtrate is produced by the kidneys each day but only about 1.5 litres of urine is excreted out.' Justify this statement.
pyq.answer: Blood is filtered under pressure in the glomerulus of every nephron, so a very large volume of filtrate, about 180 litres a day, enters the Bowman's capsules. This initial filtrate contains not only wastes but also glucose, amino acids, salts and a large amount of water, which the body cannot afford to lose. As the filtrate flows along the tubule of the nephron, these useful substances and most of the water are selectively reabsorbed into the blood capillaries around the tubule. The amount of water reabsorbed depends on how much excess water the body has and how much dissolved waste must be removed. Only the remaining fluid, about 1.5 litres of urine containing urea and other wastes, passes into the collecting duct and is excreted.

pyq.q: Explain how water and minerals are transported in plants.
pyq.answer: Water and minerals are transported through the xylem, whose vessels and tracheids in the roots, stem and leaves are interconnected to form a continuous channel. (i) Root pressure: root cells actively take up ions from the soil, creating a difference in ion concentration between the root and the soil, so water enters the root by osmosis and is pushed upward as a steady column. This is enough for short plants and is the main force at night. (ii) Transpiration pull: water evaporates from the leaf cells through the stomata, creating a suction that pulls water up from the roots through the xylem. This is the major force during the day and can lift water to the top of tall trees.

pyq.q: (a) Draw a sectional view of the human heart and label the pulmonary artery, aorta, septum and ventricles. (b) Arteries have thick walls while veins have valves. Explain. (c) Why are valves needed in the heart? (d) Leakage of blood from vessels reduces the efficiency of the pumping system. How is the leakage prevented?
pyq.answer:
(a) Draw the heart with four chambers (right and left atria above, right and left ventricles below), the septum as a vertical wall between the sides, the pulmonary artery leaving the right ventricle and the aorta leaving the left ventricle; label the four parts asked and the vena cava and pulmonary veins for completeness.

(b) Blood leaves the heart into arteries under high pressure, so arteries need thick, elastic walls to withstand it. Blood in veins flows back to the heart under low pressure and could flow backward, so veins have valves that allow flow in one direction only.

(c) Valves between the atria and ventricles, and at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery, prevent blood from flowing backwards when the atria or ventricles contract, so blood always moves in the correct direction.

(d) Blood contains platelet cells, which circulate in the blood and plug leaks at the point of injury by helping the blood to clot.

pyq.q: (a) Draw a diagram of the human excretory system and label the left kidney, ureter, urinary bladder and vena cava. (b) What is the main toxic waste that the kidney filters from the blood? (c) Name any two substances which are selectively reabsorbed from the tubules of a nephron. (d) What is the function of the urinary bladder?
pyq.answer:
(a) Draw two kidneys on either side of the aorta and vena cava, with the renal artery and renal vein entering each; a ureter from each kidney to the urinary bladder; the urethra leaving the bladder. Label the four parts asked.

(b) Urea, a nitrogenous waste formed in the liver from the breakdown of amino acids (uric acid is also removed).

(c) Glucose and amino acids (also salts and water) are selectively reabsorbed as the filtrate flows along the tubule.

(d) The urinary bladder stores the urine that comes from the kidneys through the ureters; it is muscular and under nervous control, so urine is released through the urethra when we decide to urinate.

pyq.q: (a) Describe an experiment to show that sunlight is essential for photosynthesis. (b) List the three events that occur during photosynthesis. (c) State the role of stomata in photosynthesis.
pyq.answer:
(a) Take a healthy potted plant and keep it in a dark room for two to three days so that the leaves become free of starch (destarched). Cover a part of one leaf on both sides with a strip of black paper fixed with clips, and place the plant in sunlight for about six hours. Pluck the leaf, remove the paper, boil the leaf in water for a few minutes and then in alcohol over a water bath to remove the chlorophyll. Wash the leaf and pour iodine solution on it. The part exposed to sunlight turns blue-black, showing starch is present, while the covered part does not. Since starch is formed only where light reached the leaf, sunlight is essential for photosynthesis.

(b) (i) Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll; (ii) conversion of light energy to chemical energy and splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen; (iii) reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates.

(c) Stomata are tiny pores on the leaf surface through which CO2, a raw material of photosynthesis, enters the leaf, and through which the oxygen produced is released. Their opening and closing is controlled by the guard cells.

pyq.q:
A student set up two destarched potted plants of the same size under two bell jars, sealed at the base. In jar A she placed a watch glass containing potassium hydroxide; jar B had no watch glass. Both were kept in sunlight for a few hours, after which one leaf from each plant was boiled in water, then in alcohol, and tested with iodine solution.
(i) Why were the plants destarched before the experiment?
(ii) What is the purpose of potassium hydroxide in jar A?
(iii) Which leaf will turn blue-black with iodine and why?
(iv) Why is the leaf boiled in alcohol before testing?
pyq.answer:
(i) Destarching (keeping the plant in the dark for two or three days) removes the starch already stored in the leaves, so that any starch found after the experiment must have been made during the experiment.

(ii) Potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide from the air inside jar A, so the plant in jar A has no CO2 available for photosynthesis.

(iii) The leaf from jar B turns blue-black, because that plant had CO2 available and made starch by photosynthesis; the leaf from jar A shows no colour change. This proves that CO2 is essential for photosynthesis.

(iv) Boiling in alcohol removes the green chlorophyll from the leaf so that the blue-black colour of the starch-iodine test can be seen clearly. Boiling in water first kills the cells and softens the leaf.

pyq.q:
A patient whose kidneys have failed is treated by haemodialysis. His blood is passed through a series of tubes made of a semi-permeable membrane suspended in a tank of dialysing fluid. The fluid has the same osmotic pressure as blood but contains no nitrogenous wastes. The cleaned blood is returned to the patient's body.
(i) Which waste substance mainly moves from the blood into the dialysing fluid?
(ii) Why must the dialysing fluid have the same osmotic pressure as blood?
(iii) Name the structural and functional unit of the kidney that this machine replaces, and state its two main steps of urine formation.
(iv) State one way in which the artificial kidney differs in function from a natural kidney.
pyq.answer:
(i) Urea (nitrogenous waste) diffuses from the blood into the dialysing fluid, because the fluid contains none of it.

(ii) If the osmotic pressure were different, water would move into or out of the blood across the membrane; matching it ensures that only wastes diffuse out while useful substances such as glucose and salts, present in the fluid in the same concentration as blood, are not lost.

(iii) The nephron. Urine is formed by (a) filtration of water and dissolved substances from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule under pressure, and (b) selective reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water along the tubule.

(iv) The artificial kidney removes wastes by diffusion only; there is no selective reabsorption, whereas the nephron reabsorbs useful substances and regulates the amount of water in the urine.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is the correct statement about the process of photosynthesis?
options: Oxygen released comes from carbon dioxide
Oxygen released comes from the splitting of water
Carbon dioxide is reduced in the dark only
practice_mcq.explanation: During photosynthesis water molecules are split into hydrogen and oxygen; the oxygen given out comes from water, and CO<sub>2</sub> is reduced to carbohydrate.

practice_mcq.q: Desert plants take up carbon dioxide at night because:
options: photosynthesis occurs only at night in them
their stomata are closed during the day to conserve water
CO<sub>2</sub> is available only at night
practice_mcq.explanation: To avoid water loss, desert plants keep stomata closed in the day; they store CO<sub>2</sub> as an intermediate at night and reduce it using light energy by day.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these organisms obtains food by saprophytic nutrition?
practice_mcq.explanation: Bread mould is a fungus that secretes enzymes on to dead organic matter and absorbs the digested products; Cuscuta and tapeworm are parasites, Amoeba is holozoic.

practice_mcq.q: In Paramoecium food is moved to a specific spot for ingestion by:
practice_mcq.explanation: Paramoecium has a definite shape and takes in food only at a particular spot; the cilia covering its surface sweep food to that spot.

practice_mcq.q: Which component of gastric juice protects the inner lining of the stomach from the acid?
practice_mcq.explanation: Mucus secreted by the gastric glands coats and protects the stomach lining; HCl makes the medium acidic for pepsin, and trypsin is a pancreatic enzyme.

practice_mcq.q: The small intestine of a herbivore is longer than that of a carnivore because:
options: herbivores need to absorb more water
practice_mcq.explanation: Plant food is rich in cellulose, which needs a longer time and a longer intestine to digest; meat is digested more easily, so carnivores have a shorter small intestine.

practice_mcq.q: The end products of the complete digestion of proteins and fats respectively are:
options: amino acids; fatty acids and glycerol
practice_mcq.explanation: Proteins are finally broken into amino acids and fats into fatty acids and glycerol in the small intestine; glucose is the end product of carbohydrates.

practice_mcq.q: Muscle cramps after vigorous exercise are caused by the accumulation of:
practice_mcq.explanation: When oxygen is lacking in muscle cells, pyruvate is converted to lactic acid, and its build-up causes cramps.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a feature common to the respiratory organs of all animals?
options: They are always inside the body
They have a large surface area and thin walls
They are always filled with water
practice_mcq.explanation: Whether gills, skin or lungs, respiratory surfaces are large, thin and delicate, and usually richly supplied with blood, so that gases diffuse quickly.

the ribs are lifted and the diaphragm flattens
the ribs are lifted and the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped
the ribs move down and the diaphragm flattens
practice_mcq.explanation: Lifting the ribs and flattening the diaphragm increase the volume of the chest cavity, so air is drawn into the lungs.

practice_mcq.q: Carbon dioxide is transported in the human body mainly:
options: by haemoglobin in red blood cells
in dissolved form in blood plasma
practice_mcq.explanation: CO<sub>2</sub> is more soluble in water than oxygen, so most of it travels dissolved in the plasma; haemoglobin mainly carries oxygen.

practice_mcq.q: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood but is called a vein?
practice_mcq.explanation: The pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium; it is a vein because it carries blood towards the heart.

practice_mcq.q: The chamber of the human heart that pumps blood to the lungs is the:
practice_mcq.explanation: Deoxygenated blood from the right atrium enters the right ventricle, which contracts and sends it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs.

practice_mcq.q: Normal blood pressure in a healthy adult is about:
practice_mcq.explanation: Systolic pressure (during ventricular contraction) is about 120 mm Hg and diastolic pressure (during relaxation) about 80 mm Hg, written 120/80.

practice_mcq.q: Transport of water in a tall tree during the day is mainly due to:
practice_mcq.explanation: Evaporation of water from leaf cells through stomata creates a suction, the transpiration pull, strong enough to lift water to the top of tall trees; root pressure alone is not.

practice_mcq.q: Translocation of food in phloem differs from transport in xylem because it:
practice_mcq.explanation: Sucrose is loaded into the phloem using ATP, which raises the osmotic pressure and moves material to where it is needed, in either direction.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is selectively reabsorbed from the filtrate in the tubule of a nephron?
practice_mcq.explanation: Glucose, amino acids, salts and a large amount of water are reabsorbed into the blood as the filtrate flows along the tubule; urea and other wastes remain in the urine.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a method used by plants to get rid of waste products?
options: storage of resins and gums in old xylem
practice_mcq.explanation: Plants store wastes in vacuoles, in leaves that are shed, and as resins and gums in old xylem, or excrete them into the soil; they do not form urea or have nephrons.

common_mistakes: Writing the photosynthesis equation without 'sunlight' and 'chlorophyll' over the arrow, or using 6H₂O on the left; NCERT uses 12H₂O on the left and 6H₂O on the right. The equation mark is lost either way.

Confusing breathing with respiration. Breathing is the physical intake of oxygen and release of CO₂; respiration is the chemical breakdown of glucose in cells to release energy. The examiner deducts a mark when the terms are used interchangeably.
Placing the breakdown of glucose to pyruvate in the mitochondria. It happens in the cytoplasm; only the aerobic breakdown of pyruvate occurs in the mitochondria. This is a favourite MCQ trap.
Saying bile contains enzymes, or that it digests fat. Bile has no enzyme; it emulsifies fat and makes the medium alkaline. Fat is digested by pancreatic lipase.

Swapping the pulmonary artery and aorta in the heart diagram, or labelling the left side of the heart on the left of the page. In a sectional view the left ventricle is drawn on the right of the page, and it has the thickest wall.

Writing that all arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins deoxygenated blood without the exceptions. Mention the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein, or the answer is marked incomplete in a differences table.
Attributing night-time water transport to transpiration. At night stomata are closed, so root pressure moves the water; transpiration pull works during the day.
Describing the artificial kidney as identical to the natural kidney. The dialysis machine removes wastes by diffusion but performs no reabsorption; examiners look for this difference.
Drawing a nephron with the glomerulus outside Bowman's capsule, or leaving out the collecting duct. Both are labelling marks that are easy to keep.
strategy:
This chapter is long, so divide it into the four life processes and give each one a sitting. Nutrition and transportation are the heaviest, both in content and in marks, and should get two sittings each.

Memorise the five things a marking scheme checks: the photosynthesis equation with its conditions, the three events of photosynthesis, the flow chart of glucose breakdown with the three pathways and their sites, the end products of digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, and the route of blood through the four chambers of the heart. Write each of these from memory once a day in the last week.

Practise the diagrams with a pencil, not just by looking. The heart, the alimentary canal, the excretory system and the respiratory system are almost certain to be asked in some form; the nephron, stomata and Amoeba come up less often but are quick to learn. For each one, practise labelling the parts that questions describe by function ('the chamber that receives oxygenated blood', 'the part where water is absorbed').

Prepare the differences tables in three rows each: arteries and veins, aerobic and anaerobic respiration, xylem and phloem transport, autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition, saprophytic and holozoic nutrition. A table with a heading row earns full marks faster than a paragraph.

Time in the exam: a 5-mark question with a diagram should take about 8 minutes, half of it on the diagram. Do not write more than the number of points the marks demand; a 2-mark 'two differences' question needs exactly two contrasted pairs. Answer the reasons questions ('why are ventricles thicker', 'why is bile essential', 'why do aquatic animals breathe faster') in one or two crisp sentences using the NCERT phrasing given in this guide.
